en: We are the army of the government; our enemy
is the enemy of the court, whom heaven and earth will not bear.
The man who commands the enemy
is a hero without equal, now or ever,
and the warriors who follow him
are all fierce men ready to die.
Though they have a courage that would not shame the gods,
those who have raised a rebellion that heaven does not allow
with flashing swords drawn side by side,
we must go forward ready to die.
rom: Ware wa kangun waga teki wa
teki no taishō taru mono wa
tomo ni hyōkan kesshi no shi
kijin ni hajinu yū aru mo
teki no horoburu sore made wa
notes: The first of the poem’s six stanzas; its last four lines are the refrain of every stanza.
Romanization: modified Hepburn of the words as they are read and sung; the historical kana spelling is not transliterated letter by letter (從ふ shitagau, 榮えし sakaeshi).
The poem is about the Satsuma Rebellion of 1877: the enemy’s commander is Saigō Takamori, whom it honours as a hero while condemning the rising.
Line 7: 鬼神 (kijin), fierce gods or spirits.
Line 13: 玉ちる劔, literally “swords that scatter jewels”, an old phrase for blades that flash.
